papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, more efficient students while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Across vision and language tasks, KD has evolved from simple soft-label transfers to a rich family of techniques including internal representation matching, attention- and channel-guided supervision, multi-teacher and ensemble signals, data-free and augmentation-driven methods, and architecture-aware transformations. Practical deployments combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search and must balance transfer of useful teacher information against risks such as propagating teacher errors or overfitting under limited data. The field continues to refine what teacher knowledge to transfer, how to synthesize or augment training data when it is unavailable, and how to align heterogeneous teacher–student architectures for robust, resource-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, Practical Guidance, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A range of mechanisms—soft-target matching, feature and attention imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and self- or multi-teacher schemes—enable compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and energy. Practical pipelines combine KD with architecture-aware design, pretraining or warming strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization) to meet deployment constraints. However, distillation success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and the choice of distilled signals; important open problems include robust cross-domain transfer, distillation without original data, preserving rare-token or fine-grained behaviors in language tasks, and avoiding transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a practical, versatile toolkit for compressing large models into efficient students suitable for deployment and adaptation in deep learning and NLP. When combined with representation-aware objectives, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, KD routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance; at the same time, careful method choice is required to avoid pitfalls such as degraded rare-token behavior, transferred biases, and failures under limited or private data. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central, but conditional, strategy for model compression and provides concrete recommendations for practitioners.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile technique for shrinking large neural models while preserving much of their predictive power. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and easier deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings. When combined with teacher ensembles, online or self-distillation, task-adaptive search, and careful handling of soft labels and data augmentation, distillation can deliver near-teacher accuracy while addressing scalability, robustness, and domain transfer concerns. I argue that knowledge distillation should be a first-line approach for model compression in modern NLP pipelines, supplemented by principled choices about teachers, data, and optimization to realize its full benefits.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large neural networks for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Beyond simple model-size reduction, KD enables transfer of inductive biases, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving distributed training, data-free and zero-shot compression, and the transfer of adversarial robustness. Combining logit-based distillation with feature-level mimicking and carefully chosen regularization yields high-quality small models that remain competitive on downstream tasks in NLP and broader deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from larger, often more expensive teacher models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Research over the past decade has developed a spectrum of KD objectives (soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational losses), training regimes (offline teacher-student, online co-training, self-distillation, multi-teacher schedules), and deployment-aware integrations (pre-training students, architecture-aware adapters, and combination with pruning or quantization). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while reducing parameter count and latency, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the choice of what and how to transfer. Ongoing challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, matching heterogeneous architectures, preserving low-frequency or domain-specific signals, and automating trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression: Powerful but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Its effectiveness arises from the ability to transfer different forms of knowledge (soft labels, intermediate features, attention, ensembles) and to combine distillation with data augmentation, pretraining, and task-aware objectives. However, KD is not uniformly successful: outcomes depend on teacher-student capacity alignment, the choice of distillation targets, data availability and augmentation strategy, and deployment constraints such as privacy or device heterogeneity. Careful selection of distillation signals, task-aware layer matching, and augmentation or synthetic-data strategies improve robustness; conversely, mismatches in architecture, domain shift, or heterogeneous federated settings can sharply limit benefits.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques seek to reduce the runtime, memory, and deployment costs of large deep models while retaining their predictive performance or improving other desiderata (e.g., interpretability, fairness). Across vision and language domains, methods range from classical teacher-to-student soft-target distillation to transferring intermediate representations, progressive module replacement, selective sample-driven distillation, and teacher-adaptive or teacher-free schemes. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, alignment of intermediate representations, and input-side practices (such as tailored data augmentation) can materially affect student performance. Remaining challenges include representation mismatches between teacher and student, identifying which training samples are beneficial for transfer, and adapting distillation to domain- or resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—language understanding, retrieval, visual recognition, graph-based prediction, and data-limited or privacy-constrained settings—distillation enables latency- and resource-constrained deployment. However, straightforward distillation is not a panacea: distribution shifts, heterogeneity of data and models, and absence of training data expose weaknesses that require complementary techniques (e.g., internal representation matching, layer mapping, task-aware selection, generative replay). Combining these advances yields compressed models that are both accurate and robust for real-world applications.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central model-compression approach that trains compact student models to emulate larger teacher models so that inference cost, memory, and deployment barriers are reduced while retaining much of the teacher’s predictive behavior. Research has produced a family of distillation objectives (soft-targets, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational losses), training regimes (offline, online, self-distillation, multi-teacher), and system-level integrations (pruning, structured sparsity, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical studies show well-designed distillation pipelines commonly recover a large fraction of teacher performance and sometimes improve generalization, but success depends on what knowledge is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical use therefore combines algorithmic choices with architecture-aware compression and data strategies tailored to the task and environment.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the last decade KD has diversified from soft-target matching to include intermediate representation and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. Practical compression typically combines KD with architecture-aware transformations (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies; success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data provenance, and important open problems remain in robustness, fairness, and cross-domain generalization.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or more informative models (teachers) into smaller or more efficient models (students). Research across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks has developed multiple KD objectives (soft-label matching, intermediate layer alignment, contrastive/representation losses), training regimes (offline teacher-student, online co-training, meta-learned teacher updates), and architecture-aware compression strategies (channel-wise attention, task-adaptive architecture search). Empirical and theoretical work highlights tradeoffs between bias and variance introduced by soft targets, the value of pre-training compact models before distillation, and the importance of data and augmentation choices for effective transfer. Emerging large-scale and privacy-aware deployments leverage online and federated distillation variants to reduce communication and improve reproducibility, while new approaches aim to make teachers more student-friendly or distill internal representations rather than only outputs. Key open challenges include matching representational structure across heterogeneous architectures, choosing what and when to distill, and scaling methods to very large datasets and distributed settings while preserving privacy and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD encompasses a family of techniques — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational or token-level signals, multi-teacher and self-distillation variants, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches — and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) to meet deployment constraints. Practical success requires attention to teacher–student capacity alignment, the provenance and availability of distillation data, and careful objective and schedule design; open challenges include preserving rare-token or fine-grained behavior, avoiding propagation of biases or privacy leakage, and ensuring robustness under domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), how teachers and students are aligned, and how data (real, synthetic, or absent) are handled, KD routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when practitioners explicitly address robustness, fairness, and distributional mismatch. However, KD is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the choice of distillation signal determine success, and careful objective design and evaluation are required to avoid propagating teacher errors or amplifying undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying deep models under resource constraints. Methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-layer supervision, feature mimicking, projector-based transforms, teacher-student co-training, and data- or domain-aware schemes. Distillation has been applied across modalities (vision, language, multimodal, graphs) and in settings with limited or no access to original training data. Practical advances address transfer across architectures, task-adaptive compression, and efficient architecture search, while open problems remain around distribution shift, heterogeneity of data or detectors, and preserving rare or low-frequency information.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Solis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from one or more high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple softened-logit matching into a diverse toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relation-aware losses, layer-mapping strategies for large pretrained transformers, self-distillation, curriculum-driven distillation, and complementary use with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs and enables deployment under stringent latency, memory, and privacy constraints, its success depends on careful selection of distilled signals, teacher–student co-design, data strategies, and mitigation of optimization, robustness, and distribution-shift failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Ware
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Foundation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD delivers substantial reductions in parameter count, latency, and memory while retaining much of teacher performance when applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred, teacher–student alignment, and data constraints. Its power lies in a broad toolkit—logit matching, intermediate-representation alignment, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, data-free or adversarial synthesis, and integration with pruning, quantization, or architecture search—but it is not a universal remedy: careful method selection, mitigation of distribution shift and fairness/privacy risks, and complementary compression steps are required to realize robust, production-ready students.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool: Compression, Regularization, and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression heuristic into a versatile training paradigm that enables model size reduction, improved generalization, domain adaptation, and task consolidation. Its practical success depends on both the sources of teacher supervision (final logits, intermediate representations, or multiple teachers) and how distillation is applied (sample selection, layer matching, or label design). While KD frequently yields compact, high-performing models, its benefits arise from a mixture of transferred dark knowledge and regularizing effects of soft targets; careful design choices are required to realize those benefits across settings such as language model compression, multi-task training, and privacy-constrained or heterogeneous environments.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. Practitioners apply KD not only as a logits-matching loss but as a system-level design primitive that includes representation matching, multi-teacher fusion, data and curriculum design, and combination with pruning and quantization. Its empirical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer (soft labels, intermediate features, relational signals), how to map teacher signals to potentially heterogeneous students, and how to handle limited or private data. While KD often yields compact models with near-teacher performance and useful regularization effects, limitations remain: imperfect teacher signals, optimization challenges, robustness and fairness transfer, and domain-shift or data-scarce scenarios. Current best practices emphasize task-aware selection of distilled signals, layer/projector alignment, and hybrid pipelines that combine KD with other compression techniques to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD methods differ in what is transferred (softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals) and in training protocols (offline teacher supervision, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants). In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and when practitioner choices account for teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and target-task constraints. While KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision and language tasks, its limitations include sensitivity to optimization dynamics, degradation on rare or safety-critical behaviors, and challenges in data-free or privacy-constrained settings. The field offers pragmatic recipes—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning representations, and using data or synthetic surrogates—that produce deployable compact models, but outstanding research questions remain about principled teacher design, robustness under distribution shift, and data-free distillation quality.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A diverse set of KD mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature alignment, attention- and relation-based signals, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data synthesis—has been developed and combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many vision and language tasks, while remaining sensitive to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, domain shift, and robustness concerns. Practical pipelines therefore co-design student architectures, distillation targets, and data handling strategies to achieve the best trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has evolved from logit-matching for model compression into a multifaceted toolkit that includes intermediate-representation matching, attention- and channel-level transfers, teacher ensembles, data- and teacher-free variants, and task- or domain-aware adaptations. Practical success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment (capacity and architecture), the availability and provenance of data, and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design). While KD often preserves much of the teacher’s performance and can improve generalization through soft-target regularization, important limits remain around distribution shift, low-frequency token or class handling, and preserving robustness and fairness under compression.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an established approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple logit-matching into a toolkit that includes intermediate-feature imitation, attention and relation transfer, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schedules, and data- or privacy-aware variants. When combined with architecture-aware choices, pruning, quantization, and data augmentation, KD frequently yields compact models that approach teacher performance, but practical effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity alignment, availability and form of data, and careful selection of distillation signals. Open challenges include reliable transfer under distribution shift, preserving rare/fine-grained behaviors, fairness and bias mitigation, and principled methods for heterogeneous teacher–student pairings.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable smaller or faster models to retain much of the performance of larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or task-specific inductive biases. Work in this area spans supervised soft-target matching, intermediate-layer representation transfer, many-to-many layer alignment, data-free distillation, multi-teacher and ensemble-derived strategies, and online/distributed variants that exploit parallelism. Applications include compressing large pretrained language models for downstream NLP tasks, accelerating inference for computer vision and generative models, and producing interpretable or privacy-preserving compact models for healthcare and on-device deployment. Important trade-offs involve what form of knowledge is transferred (logits, activations, relations), access to training data, robustness to domain heterogeneity, and how to balance capacity, efficiency, and generalization in student models.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Benefits, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and natural language processing. KD methods transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from teachers to students using a variety of signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure) and configurations (single- or multi-teacher, online/offline, data-driven or data-free). When combined with complementary compression techniques and appropriate data strategies, KD routinely yields compact models with substantially reduced inference cost while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. However, its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, the type and availability of data used for transfer, optimization dynamics, and downstream robustness, and so KD is best applied as one element of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Pragmatic, but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach that enables deploying large neural models by transferring richer supervisory signals from teacher models into smaller students. Empirical and methodological work across vision, language, speech, and distributed settings shows KD can achieve large reductions in size and latency while retaining most of a teacher’s performance, but its success depends on matching what is distilled, how teacher and student are paired, and which data and training protocols are used. Best outcomes arise when KD is combined with targeted representation matching, data strategies, and task- or architecture-aware choices; conversely, naive application can propagate teacher errors or underperform when constrained by data, domain shift, or privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Current Understandings of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used model compression paradigm in which a smaller student model is trained to capture the behavior of a larger teacher model. It has been applied across domains (vision, NLP, recommender systems, medical imaging) to reduce model size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Work in the field explores what is transferred (soft outputs, internal representations, feature relations), how to improve transfer (adversarial samples, contrastive objectives, structural transformations), and how to address practical constraints (absence of original data, domain shift, privacy, fairness and robustness). Empirical results show KD often yields substantial memory and runtime benefits with modest accuracy loss and can be combined with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Yet KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, imperfect teacher signals, and mismatches between teacher and student capacity can limit how closely a student matches a teacher; research continues into theoretical explanations and robust, data-efficient methods.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural teachers into smaller student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, KD techniques include soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention- or relation-based alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher fusion, and data- or domain-aware variations. Empirical work shows that distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet deployment constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and training objectives. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, transferring robustness and inductive biases, and handling heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive environments.

papers_seen.author: Vance
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a unified, pragmatic pathway to compress large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. When applied thoughtfully—selecting what to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, augmenting or synthesizing data when necessary, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques—KD consistently yields large efficiency gains (memory, compute, latency) while retaining much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and multimodal settings. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and robustness concerns, and practical pipelines must address these limits through curriculum design, data-aware augmentation, and careful choice of distillation targets.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s predictive power. A variety of mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate feature imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and architecture-aware search—enable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, model size, and privacy. Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary methods (pretraining of compact architectures, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, and privacy-preserving synthesis) and tailor choices to data availability, task constraints, and target hardware. Despite broad empirical success, open issues remain around transferring robustness and rare-token behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing distillation pipelines that are robust under limited or private data.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Robbins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performance models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A heterogeneous family of techniques—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, multi-teacher schedules, data-free synthesis, and task- or architecture-aware adaptations—enables compact models to approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. Effective application requires careful choice of distilled signals, attention to teacher–student capacity and data availability, and often combining distillation with complementary compression methods; limitations remain around optimization difficulties, distribution shift, privacy-sensitive scenarios, and reliably transferring robustness and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher to student. A diverse set of approaches extend the basic soft-label paradigm to include internal representation matching, layer-wise and attention-guided alignment, task-aware selection of distilled features, data-free or zero-shot synthesis of training examples, augmentation-driven consistency, multi-teacher and ensemble transfer, adversarial learning objectives, and architecture search tailored to downstream tasks. These techniques improve inference efficiency while aiming to preserve accuracy, generalization, and task-specific behavior; they also enable distillation in settings with limited or no access to original training data and in generation tasks. Ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous architectures, selecting which teacher knowledge to preserve for a given student capacity and task, and designing robust distilled models that generalize across domains and data shifts.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. KD enables deploying compact models that retain much of teacher performance, supports cross-modal and task-specific transfers, and can be adapted to privacy- and data-constrained settings. While highly effective in practice, KD’s outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and objective design; realizing its full potential requires targeted methodological choices such as feature-level matching, multi-teacher fusion, adversarial data synthesis, and privacy-preserving mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: The Versatility and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students while preserving much of their performance. Across domains — including reinforcement learning, vision, generative modeling, and language — distillation can accelerate inference, enable deployment on constrained devices, and transfer capabilities such as domain adaptation or lifelong learning. However, its effectiveness depends on choices about teacher-student pairing, data availability and augmentation, sample selection, and training protocols; it also interacts with privacy and heterogeneity constraints. A balanced approach that combines principled distillation objectives, appropriate data strategies (including data-free methods when necessary), and curriculum or annealing schedules yields the best tradeoffs between compactness and retained performance.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core First-Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP — Powerful, Context‑Dependent, and Best Used in Integrated Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile method for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When done beyond naïve soft-label copying—e.g., via intermediate-representation matching, attention or layer alignment, and careful teacher–student design—KD routinely delivers large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. Its strongest role is as a first-line, representation-aware strategy that is combined with complementary compression techniques and data strategies. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors and distributional failures. Practical deployment therefore requires principled recipes, diagnostics for failure modes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Path for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. By transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone—ranging from softened logits to intermediate features, attention maps, and multi-teacher signals—KD enables compact models that preserve much of teacher performance while supporting complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture-aware transforms). KD also enables specialized workflows when data are limited or private (e.g., data-free distillation) and can be adapted to preserve robustness or domain-specific expertise. Realizing KD’s full potential requires careful choices about the form of knowledge, teacher–student alignment, and training curricula, but when these are handled methodically KD provides a practical, general toolkit for deploying high-quality compact models in resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Principled Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' predictive power. KD is most effective when it goes beyond naïve soft-label copying: matching internal representations, aligning inputs and tokenization, choosing appropriate data or synthesis strategies, and adapting teacher updates or curricula all materially affect transfer quality. KD should be used as part of a broader compression pipeline (architecture design, quantization, pruning, or data strategies) and with explicit checks for rare-token behavior, fairness, and robustness. When applied with these considerations, KD reliably produces compact models suitable for production constraints in vision, language, and other modalities.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Benefits, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and natural language processing. KD methods transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from teachers to students using a variety of signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure) and configurations (single- or multi-teacher, online/offline, data-driven or data-free). When combined with complementary compression techniques and appropriate data strategies, KD routinely yields compact models with substantially reduced inference cost while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. However, its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, the type and availability of data used for transfer, optimization dynamics, and downstream robustness, and so KD is best applied as one element of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and practically central approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal settings. KD operates via multiple types of transferred signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure) and training regimes (offline teacher-to-student, online peer distillation, ensemble-to-student). In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) and when design choices about student capacity, data, and objectives are aligned with deployment constraints. Despite strong empirical success, open challenges remain around preserving robustness, fairness and rare-token behaviors, operating under limited or private data, and principled selection of what and how to distill.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. A broad set of practical recipes—including logit (soft-target) supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, many-to-many layer alignment, data-free/zero-shot synthesis, and joint use with architecture search, pruning, or quantization—enable deployment of compact models across vision, language, and graph tasks. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while reducing compute and memory, but effectiveness depends on the choice of transfer target, availability or synthesis of suitable data, student architecture, and training dynamics. Key open issues remain around principled explanations for when distillation helps, reliably transferring robustness and fairness properties, privacy-aware distillation, and automating student design for specific resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Lambert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the original model's utility. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, and generation tasks show that carefully designed distillation—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate feature and relational transfer, online co-training, and progressive module replacement—enables large reductions in latency and memory with modest accuracy loss. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and augmentation, and targeted mitigation of risks such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, and privacy leakage. Treating KD as a system-level primitive and combining it with complementary compression and data strategies yields the best practical outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an established approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple logit-matching into a toolkit that includes intermediate-feature imitation, attention and relation transfer, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schedules, and data- or privacy-aware variants. When combined with architecture-aware choices, pruning, quantization, and data augmentation, KD frequently yields compact models that approach teacher performance, but practical effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity alignment, availability and form of data, and careful selection of distillation signals. Open challenges include reliable transfer under distribution shift, preserving rare/fine-grained behaviors, fairness and bias mitigation, and principled methods for heterogeneous teacher–student pairings.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Multifaceted, and Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their predictive power. When combined with complementary strategies—task-aware objectives, intermediate representation matching, online or distributed schemes, and teacher-student co-design—KD supports deployment on resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive environments. Nonetheless, its effectiveness depends strongly on teacher-student capacity alignment, data availability (including few-shot or data-free regimes), and the choice of distilled signals; recognizing these dependencies leads to principled best practices that balance fidelity, robustness, and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). Advances span logit- and feature-based matching, multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, data-free and federated scenarios, and domain- or task-specific adaptations in NLP. Practical work shows KD can yield large reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance, but design choices (what to match, how to weight teachers, whether data are available, and deployment constraints) strongly affect outcomes. Remaining challenges include robustness to domain shift, privacy and communication constraints in distributed settings, and principled handling of teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. When thoughtfully applied — selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques and data strategies — distillation enables large reductions in compute and memory with modest performance loss. However, KD is not universally sufficient on its own: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and provenance, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines therefore treat distillation as a core element of a broader compression strategy, integrating pretraining, representation-aware objectives, multi-teacher curricula, and privacy- or data-constrained methods to produce robust, efficient models for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Bounded Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and natural language tasks. KD techniques — from logits matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, multi-teacher schedules, adversarial and data-free variants — enable large reductions in size and latency while retaining much of a teacher's performance. However, realizing these gains in practice requires task- and student-aware design choices, attention to data and privacy constraints, and explicit strategies to mitigate transferred fragilities. KD is therefore an essential tool in the compression toolbox, but not a universal remedy: careful method selection and evaluation under deployment constraints determine success.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Practical Case for Richer Knowledge Distillation in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a necessary and practical tool for compressing large models and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings, but its value depends critically on what is distilled and how. Soft-label matching transfers useful "dark knowledge" from ensembles, yet by itself often fails to capture internal structure, handle domain or data heterogeneity, or operate when original data are unavailable. Combining soft labels with internal- and feature-level guidance, architecture- and task-aware compression, and data- or privacy-aware generation strategies yields more robust, compact models that retain teacher performance across NLP and broader deep learning tasks.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable route to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their predictive capability. KD achieves favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across modalities and tasks, but its real-world success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and explicit handling of robustness, fairness, and deployment constraints. A pragmatic approach treats KD as a core tool that should routinely be combined with complementary compression, data, and training strategies.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a pragmatic and flexible approach to compressing large neural models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. KD enables substantial reductions in size and compute while retaining much of a teacher model's performance, and it adapts well to modalities from vision to speech and to task-specific constraints in NLP. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, mismatches between teacher and student, and the potential for poorer outcomes when distilling inappropriate teacher signals require careful method selection and evaluation. Best practice therefore combines tailored distillation architectures, curriculum or multi-teacher strategies, privacy-aware mechanisms where needed, and awareness of when label-smoothing or teacher-free alternatives are preferable.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teacher’s performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation can be combined with architectural replacement, layer mapping, and task-adaptive search to produce compact models that meet latency and capacity constraints. However, the benefits of distillation depend strongly on teacher quality, data complexity, and which examples or representations are used for transfer; naive application can propagate teacher errors or harm low-frequency predictions. Careful design—using task-aware compression, selective or mixed supervision, and targeted remedies for dataset artifacts—enables distillation to deliver efficient, robust models for real-world NLP and vision systems.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining as much task performance as possible. Over the past decade KD has evolved from matching softened output distributions to a broad set of practical techniques that include intermediate representation matching, layer-wise alignment, online and multi-teacher training, data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning and quantization. Empirical work shows KD can substantially shrink model size and latency for vision and language systems and can be adapted for privacy-sensitive and distributed settings; however, its success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and the availability or synthesis of suitable training data, and it faces open challenges in robustness, cross-domain generalization, and heterogeneous deployment.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfer knowledge from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels — softened output distributions, intermediate feature or attention imitation, and relational or layer-wise alignment — and composes naturally with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD yields substantial gains in latency, memory, and energy for deployed systems, but its success depends on careful design choices related to what is distilled, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability, and robustness or fairness requirements. Practical deployment treats KD as a core element of a hybrid compression pipeline, with task-aware signal selection, student-aware teacher design, and targeted remedies for distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, adversarial vulnerability, and privacy risks.
