papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models so as to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD spans soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, layer-wise alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or zero-shot methods for cases where original training data are unavailable. In practice KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression building blocks (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when design choices account for teacher–student capacity, data availability, and task-specific objectives. Remaining practical challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, preserving fine-grained behaviors (e.g., rare tokens or safety-critical outputs), and principled methods for data-free or privacy-sensitive distillation.

papers_seen.author: Burke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical and flexible pathway to convert large, high‑performing models into compact students suitable for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When matched to student capacity and task constraints, distillation can preserve most of a teacher’s performance while enabling complementary compression (quantization, pruning) and deployment strategies. Realistic application of KD requires attention to what signals are transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention, or relational structure), how teacher and student inputs and architectures are aligned, and how limited or synthetic data are used. KD also carries risks—propagation of teacher errors, loss of rare‑token behavior, domain shift sensitivity, and privacy issues—that mandate task‑aware design and evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A spectrum of distillation signals—soft logits, intermediate features and attention, relational/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis—enables compact models that often retain most of teacher performance. Empirical results across NLP, speech, graph learning, and vision show KD’s practical value, while theoretical and empirical analyses point to mechanisms (soft-target regularization, ensemble-induced ‘‘dark knowledge’’, and representation shaping) and to limits tied to student capacity, data alignment, optimization dynamics, and robustness under distribution shift. Practical deployment requires careful selection of what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design).

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Understanding and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. It encompasses soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and training-time adaptations that account for student capacity and deployment constraints. In practice KD is combined with complementary methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, and data-free synthesis) to meet latency, memory, or privacy requirements. KD is effective across vision, language, generative models, and view- or modality-specific tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student compatibility, available data, and careful choice of distillation objectives and schedules; open challenges remain in robustness, rare-token behavior, fairness, and theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Mcmillan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Indispensable but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the original performance. KD has proven effective across modalities and tasks, and modern practice extends beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-representation alignment, multi-teacher fusion, data-free approaches, and training-time strategies that make teachers more amenable to transfer. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: distribution shifts, limited or absent training data, teacher–student mismatch, and adversarial concerns require complementary techniques and careful design. When combined with task-aware selection of distilled signals, student-friendly teacher training, and data- or representation-aware remedies, KD becomes a practical backbone for deployment under latency, compute, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed a spectrum of KD mechanisms — soft-target (logit) transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and progressive schedules, and task- or deployment-aware pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, or architecture design. Empirical evidence shows that carefully designed distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in inference cost, but success depends on teacher–student capacity alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and task-specific considerations (e.g., preserving fine-grained sequence behavior or relational structure). Privacy, heterogeneity of deployment devices, and data-scarce regimes motivate variants with differential privacy, few-shot or cross-layer schemes, and heterogeneous multi-model sharing to ensure inclusive and practical compression.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Dependent Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. It delivers meaningful trade-offs between model size, latency, and retained performance when paired with appropriate distillation targets, student-aware design, and complementary compression techniques. However, KD’s success is conditional: it depends on teacher-student capacity alignment, data availability (including privacy constraints), the choice of distilled signals (soft targets versus intermediate features), and optimization practices. Best outcomes arise from task-aware distillation pipelines that combine soft-target transfer, representation-level supervision, and pragmatic strategies such as data synthesis, augmentation, or architecture-aware adjustments.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from pre-trained teachers. The approach spans soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free workflows. Empirical results show KD often recovers much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and optimization protocols. Ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors, maintaining robustness and fairness under distribution shift, and operating when original training data is limited or unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Gates
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Capabilities, Variants, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a practical, multipurpose toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. By transferring information at the output level (soft targets) and across intermediate representations, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. KD is most effective when treated as part of a broader compression strategy that aligns distillation signals to student capacity, leverages data-aware or data-free variants when needed, and combines distillation with pruning, quantization, or architecture redesign. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, data availability and match, and careful choice of what and how to transfer; open problems include preserving rare behaviors, robustness under distribution shift, and principled automation of trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical, flexible route to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. KD spans multiple mechanisms — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation transfer, layer-wise or progressive replacement, privacy- and data-aware variants — and can be combined with structural compression such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is highly effective in many realistic settings but is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, what form of knowledge is transferred, data availability (including few-shot or privacy-constrained scenarios), and careful optimization and evaluation. Viewed as a central yet context-sensitive tool, KD should be a default component of compression pipelines, applied in concert with complementary methods and guarded by targeted diagnostics for robustness and rare-token or out-of-distribution behavior.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural teachers into smaller student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, KD techniques include soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention- or relation-based alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher fusion, and data- or domain-aware variations. Empirical work shows that distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet deployment constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and training objectives. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, transferring robustness and inductive biases, and handling heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive environments.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated framework that enables transferring predictive power from large, expensive models to smaller, deployable ones. KD supports diverse practical constraints — absent training data, limited downstream-task data, domain shifts, multi-task settings, and architectural mismatches — and couples naturally with automated model search and targeted feature imitation. By viewing KD as a family of techniques (logit transfer, feature mimicking, adversarial-sample guidance, synthetic-data distillation, and teacher-ensemble strategies) practitioners can compress models while retaining or even improving task-relevant inductive structure and generalization.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and language. A diverse set of distillation recipes—soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, self- and online-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and data-free synthesis—enables trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy. Success depends on co-designing teacher and student architectures, selecting appropriate transfer signals, handling data availability or privacy constraints, and integrating complementary compression methods. Remaining gaps include robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or safety-critical behaviors, and principled theory to predict when particular distillation strategies will succeed in production.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Research spans algorithmic advances in teacher–student objectives, architecture-aware compression, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Practical work shows gains from combining KD with data augmentation, many-to-many layer mappings, and architecture search, while complementary efforts address data-free and privacy-preserving distillation. Remaining challenges include imperfect teachers, data heterogeneity, and adapting compression to task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. KD encompasses a family of techniques—logit matching, feature- and attention-level transfer, multi-teacher and ensemble-to-student schemes, and hybrid pipelines combined with pruning or architecture modification—that make it adaptable to diverse deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy). When applied with attention to the form of transferred knowledge, teacher quality, and data strategies, KD yields compact models suitable for production NLP and cross-modal systems; however, careful design is required to avoid pitfalls such as degraded calibration, transferred biases, or student–teacher mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of teacher performance. Research across vision, speech, translation, and NLP tasks has developed multiple KD objectives (soft logits, intermediate-feature matching, attention or projector-based alignment), training regimes (offline teacher–student, self-distillation, multi-teacher, adversarial transfer), and data strategies (data-free, distilled datasets, and hybrid authentic/synthetic training). Empirical and theoretical work explains why KD often improves student generalization (dark-knowledge regularization, transferred inductive biases) while also documenting limitations (capacity mismatch, teacher error propagation, distributional/low-frequency failures) and practical remedies. Best practice is to treat KD as a flexible toolkit and combine it with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to reproduce useful behavior of larger teacher models so that deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints becomes practical. KD encompasses a family of techniques — from matching teacher output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure — and is commonly combined with complementary compressions such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows that, when matched to student capacity and data availability, distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Practical success depends on choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data access (including data-free alternatives), and robustness or fairness requirements; remaining challenges concern principled objective design, optimization under capacity mismatch, and reliable transfer of robustness and rare-token/long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models or ensembles into smaller, efficient student models. KD methods span soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, multi-teacher or online schemes, and data- or privacy-aware variants; they are frequently combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical results across vision, speech, language, generative, and 3D tasks show that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation signals, teacher–student alignment, and data strategies are chosen appropriately, but open problems remain around data-free scenarios, robustness to distribution shift, fairness, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks, KD variants — including soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, self-distillation, and progressive module replacement — have been shown to reduce inference cost and memory while retaining much of the teacher's utility. Practical deployments combine KD with complementary techniques (data augmentation, low-precision numerics, teacher adaptation, and data-filtering) and must manage failure modes stemming from teacher–student capacity mismatch, data availability, and domain shift. The field continues to refine what knowledge to transfer, how to perform transfer efficiently, and how to preserve robustness and privacy in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line, System‑Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and multifaceted approach to compressing large models into compact students that can be deployed under latency, memory, and compute constraints. When treated as a system-level pipeline rather than a single loss term, KD—combined with careful student design, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques—yields strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. At the same time, the method’s reliability depends on teacher quality, data alignment, and architectural matching, so practitioners must evaluate distillation outcomes under realistic deployment constraints and data heterogeneity.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. When combined with representation-level objectives, architecture-aware techniques, and deployment-aware protocols, KD preserves much of teacher performance while enabling real-world constraints such as latency, memory, and device heterogeneity to be met. Best practices include selecting appropriate distilled signals (beyond soft labels), pretraining or warming students, and aligning objectives with deployment constraints. Despite strong empirical success across modalities, open challenges remain in handling data heterogeneity, domain shift, privacy-sensitive settings, and the automated design of student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces the cost of deploying large deep models by transferring information from high-capacity teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of KD variants—soft-target matching, internal-feature and attention matching, multi-teacher or ensemble guidance, online and meta-learned teaching, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches—enable tradeoffs among size, latency, and retained performance. Practical deployments commonly combine KD with architecture-aware transformations (pruning, quantization, architecture redesign), data-management strategies, and training schedules to address constraints such as limited data, device heterogeneity, privacy, and fairness. While KD often produces strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices about what and how to transfer, student capacity and architecture, and the provenance of training data; persistent challenges include domain shift, teacher errors, preserving rare behaviors, and avoiding unintentional transfer of bias.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, expressive models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple logit-matching to a diverse toolkit that includes feature- and layer-level supervision, multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, self-distillation and teacher optimization, and approaches that enable data-free or privacy-preserving compression. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling faster inference and smaller footprints; however, practical success depends on choices about objectives, alignment between teacher and student, data availability, and robustness to domain shift. Open directions include stronger theoretical characterization of what is transferred, principled treatment of heterogeneous teachers, and tighter integration of KD with quantization, pruning, and privacy mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Practical, but Not a Panacea
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are essential tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. A wide family of methods — from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature transfer, projector-based alignment, data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning or architecture search — let practitioners trade compute and memory for modest accuracy loss. However, KD’s effectiveness depends on optimization, data alignment, and the choice of distilled signals; it can replicate undesirable teacher behaviors and fails when teacher–student mismatch or data constraints are not addressed. Practical deployment therefore requires selecting KD variants that match application constraints and combining distillation with complementary compression and robustness techniques.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students that are suitable for deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. A spectrum of KD techniques—from matching softened teacher outputs to aligning intermediate representations, multi-teacher supervision, and architecture-aware student design—has been shown to recover much of teacher performance when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical success depends on choices of distillation signal, data availability and alignment between teacher and student; practical systems also require attention to computational cost during distillation and to domain or heterogeneity challenges in distributed settings. Remaining gaps include principled selection of teacher signals for specific tasks, reliable data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, and methods that scale distillation quality and efficiency simultaneously.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information from teacher models. KD encompasses a family of techniques — matching teacher logits (soft targets), aligning intermediate features or attention maps, online or mutual distillation, self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants — that are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance in vision and language tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality and specialization, student capacity and architecture, availability and alignment of data, and optimization choices; naive distillation can propagate teacher errors or fail under strong teacher–student mismatch. Practical pipelines therefore select distillation signals and schedules appropriate to task and deployment constraints, often pairing KD with complementary compression techniques to trade compute and size for modest predictive degradation.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s predictive power. A variety of mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate feature imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and architecture-aware search—enable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, model size, and privacy. Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary methods (pretraining of compact architectures, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, and privacy-preserving synthesis) and tailor choices to data availability, task constraints, and target hardware. Despite broad empirical success, open issues remain around transferring robustness and rare-token behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing distillation pipelines that are robust under limited or private data.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation in Modern Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a foundational technique for compressing large neural models while retaining much of their performance. Across vision and language tasks, distillation can act both as a compression mechanism and as a regularizer, and it integrates naturally with complementary strategies such as architecture search, layer-wise alignment, representation matching, data augmentation, pruning, and deployment-aware methods. When applied thoughtfully—matching teacher and student representations, tuning the signal provided by soft labels, and adapting to task or device constraints—distillation enables practical, high-performing compressed models suitable for production and edge settings.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. KD is applicable across modalities and tasks, from machine translation and reading comprehension to distributed training and privacy-sensitive deployment. Success depends on aligning teacher and student representations, selecting appropriate knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention, contrastive signals), and matching methods to constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous devices, or privacy requirements. Theoretical analyses and practical advances both show that careful design choices — including attention-based matching, layer projection, task-aware filtering, online collaboration, multi-teacher weighting, and privacy-aware perturbation — materially affect outcomes and trade-offs between fidelity, efficiency, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. When thoughtfully applied — selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques and data strategies — distillation enables large reductions in compute and memory with modest performance loss. However, KD is not universally sufficient on its own: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and provenance, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines therefore treat distillation as a core element of a broader compression strategy, integrating pretraining, representation-aware objectives, multi-teacher curricula, and privacy- or data-constrained methods to produce robust, efficient models for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Theory, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely used approach to compressing large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. KD methods span soft-logit matching, ensemble distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, self- and multi-teacher schedules, and privacy- or data-aware variants. Empirical results across vision and language tasks show that carefully chosen distillation targets and student–teacher alignment can achieve large reductions in inference cost with modest loss (and sometimes gains) in performance. However, practical success depends on capacity-matching, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of failure modes such as propagation of teacher errors, degraded rare-token behavior in NLP, and privacy concerns. KD performs best as a component of a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture choices, pruning/quantization, and data-centric strategies.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically effective approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster students for deployment. When combined with complementary compression techniques and task-aware choices about what and how to transfer, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. At the same time, careful attention to data availability, teacher–student mismatch, and domain shift is required to preserve robustness and rare or domain-specific behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach for producing compact models that meet deployment constraints in compute, memory, latency, and privacy. When integrated with complementary techniques (layer mapping, data strategies, adversarial training, and architecture-aware design), KD enables substantial compression with modest performance loss across vision and language tasks. Realizing these gains requires deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. This paper argues that KD should be a first-line strategy in compression pipelines while outlining practical caveats and design recommendations for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost while attempting to preserve predictive performance. KD encompasses a range of mechanisms — soft-target (logit) matching, feature and intermediate-layer imitation, attention- or channel-based guidance, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, self-distillation, and data- or device-aware variants — and is applied across modalities including vision and language. Empirical work shows KD can yield substantial reductions in parameters and latency with modest accuracy loss, and in some settings can improve student generalization. Practical deployment couples KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and requires careful design choices around teacher-student alignment, data availability, and task-specific objectives.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) unifies many successful strategies for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones that retain most of their performance. KD methods are adaptable across settings—from single-task NLP compression to large-scale distributed training and federated learning—and recent advances address core challenges such as teacher-student alignment, multi-teacher fusion, data scarcity, and domain shift. By combining architectural mapping, task-aware selection of distilled signals, dynamic teacher weighting, and online or data-free schemes, KD enables deployment of strong models in latency-, compute-, and privacy-constrained settings while exposing clear directions for further research.

papers_seen.author: Merritt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully — choosing what to transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps), aligning teacher and student capacity, and addressing data constraints — KD enables strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of appropriate data, and explicit safeguards for robustness and fairness. Combining KD with complementary techniques (architecture search, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, and privacy-aware protocols) and adopting task-adaptive distillation pipelines yields the most reliable real-world outcomes.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal information from teacher models. KD methods range from matching softened teacher logits to aligning intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, and are commonly combined with complementary engineering strategies (architecture design, pretraining of compact models, quantization, and data augmentation). Empirical evidence shows distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability and augmentation, and the relative strength and role of the teacher; these choices shape practical tradeoffs in robustness, fairness, and cross-distribution generalization.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces the cost of deploying large deep models by transferring information from high-capacity teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of KD variants—soft-target matching, internal-feature and attention matching, multi-teacher or ensemble guidance, online and meta-learned teaching, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches—enable tradeoffs among size, latency, and retained performance. Practical deployments commonly combine KD with architecture-aware transformations (pruning, quantization, architecture redesign), data-management strategies, and training schedules to address constraints such as limited data, device heterogeneity, privacy, and fairness. While KD often produces strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices about what and how to transfer, student capacity and architecture, and the provenance of training data; persistent challenges include domain shift, teacher errors, preserving rare behaviors, and avoiding unintentional transfer of bias.

papers_seen.author: Shelton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Complementary Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD delivers real efficiency gains when its targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals) and training protocols are matched to student capacity and deployment constraints. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its best use is as the central element of a compression pipeline that explicitly addresses teacher–student alignment, data availability, robustness, and complementary compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical success requires careful design of distilled signals, data or synthetic-data strategies, and evaluation under realistic distributional and fairness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques compress large, high-performance models into smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from a teacher to a student. Recent work spans many complementary strategies — logit/soft-target matching, feature and layer-wise distillation, structural and channel-level transformations, data-free generation of proxy inputs, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and task-aware filtering — and addresses practical concerns such as cross-domain transfer, limited compute, and maintaining task performance in NLP settings. Progress includes specialized algorithms for pre-trained language model compression, algorithmic and architectural enhancements that reduce capacity gaps, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Together these developments offer a toolkit for deploying compact models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive environments while preserving most of the original model performance.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring useful predictive and representational knowledge from teacher models to students. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., layer mapping, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, pruning, and quantization) and guided by student-aware design and fairness/robustness constraints, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of a teacher's accuracy. Practical deployment of KD requires attention to data availability, teacher quality, and domain-specific constraints to avoid propagating undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Multi‑Strategy Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach to compressing large models into smaller, efficient students. When treated as a toolbox of complementary methods—logit-level supervision, representation matching, layer alignment, multi-teacher schedules, data synthesis, and privacy-aware mechanisms—KD enables compact models to approach the performance of larger teachers while meeting real-world constraints on latency, memory, and data access. At the same time, distillation outcomes depend on teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices; addressing these limits requires careful method selection and integration with complementary compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models to emulate larger teacher models so that inference cost, memory, and latency are reduced while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a diverse toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and channel-wise transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schedules, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. KD is most effective when matched to student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints and is typically combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) to meet practical requirements. Important limits remain — including sensitivity to teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, robustness and fairness concerns, and data scarcity — motivating hybrid methods and careful evaluation in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient students while retaining much of their predictive performance. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners use KD to achieve lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and easier deployment under resource, privacy, or heterogeneity constraints. Effective distillation combines choices about which knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention maps), how to align teacher and student layers, how to generate or select training data, and how to adapt architectures to task requirements. While KD often succeeds when paired with complementary techniques (e.g., architecture search, ensembling, data augmentation), its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability and quality, and targeted objectives that reflect downstream tasks. Recognizing the mechanisms and limits of KD helps practitioners design robust compression pipelines that balance efficiency, accuracy, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD encompasses logit-level soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational or ensemble signals, and many practical variants (online, self-distillation, data-free). When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student co-design, KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for classification, sequence tasks, retrieval, and generative systems. However, KD is not universally effective: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and distributional match, and the choice of distillation signals; open problems include reliable distillation without original data, preserving low-frequency or rare behaviors in NLP, and avoiding transfer of undesirable properties such as biases or fragility.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a set of techniques to transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students). Approaches vary from soft-label supervision and internal representation matching to data-free synthesis, task-adaptive architecture search, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols. Empirical results across vision and language tasks show distilled students can approach teacher performance while enabling deployment under computational, storage, privacy, or bandwidth constraints; open challenges include robustness, heterogeneity of data and models, and few-shot or label-scarce regimes.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has diversified from matching soft logits to a family of techniques that include intermediate feature and attention imitation, projector- or layer-aware mapping, ensemble and curriculum strategies, and data-free or privacy-preserving variants. Practical pipelines typically combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic examples) to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints, while facing challenges from teacher–student mismatch, data availability, and robustness or bias transfer.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical paradigm for compressing and accelerating large deep models by transferring information from a cumbersome teacher to a compact student. Across modalities and tasks—supervised classification, representation learning, structured prediction, and generation—research shows KD can produce lightweight models that approach teacher performance, recover performance of small architectures, or enable new deployment constraints (privacy, federated settings). However, success depends critically on what is distilled (outputs, intermediate representations, attention across layers), the data or metadata available for distillation, and the learning dynamics between teacher and student. Open challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, sensitivity to data heterogeneity, and designing teachers or distillation procedures that reliably transfer the right kind of knowledge for a target student capacity and deployment setting.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining as much task performance as possible. Over the past decade KD has evolved from matching softened output distributions to a broad set of practical techniques that include intermediate representation matching, layer-wise alignment, online and multi-teacher training, data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning and quantization. Empirical work shows KD can substantially shrink model size and latency for vision and language systems and can be adapted for privacy-sensitive and distributed settings; however, its success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and the availability or synthesis of suitable training data, and it faces open challenges in robustness, cross-domain generalization, and heterogeneous deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Context‑Sensitive Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically grounded approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely produces favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when practitioners choose what signals to transfer (logits, intermediate features, relational signals), align teacher and student architectures, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on data availability, teacher quality and design, teacher–student compatibility, and evaluation under distribution shift and fairness constraints. Responsible deployment therefore requires principled choices about distilled signals, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy.
