papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A broad family of KD techniques—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, using multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and synthesizing data when originals are unavailable—has proven effective across vision, language, and other modalities. Practical success depends on co-designing what is transferred, student architecture and capacity, and data strategies; important open problems include robust transfer under domain shift, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behaviors, data-free and privacy-sensitive distillation, and principled combinations of KD with other compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Stein
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, widely used family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large "teacher" models to smaller "student" models so that students approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. KD encompasses transferring softened outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive signals, and it is often combined with architecture modification, pruning, quantization, and data strategies (including data-free or synthetic-data approaches). Empirical and conceptual work shows KD reliably improves accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision, language, graph, and cross-domain tasks, but its success is context dependent: teacher quality and compatibility, student capacity, availability and domain match of data, and explicit handling of robustness, privacy, and distribution shift are central determinants of outcome.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential and Practical, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing parameter count and inference cost, but its reliability depends on choices about what to distill, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited, heterogeneous, or private data. Realistic deployment requires combining KD with complementary compression techniques, adapting the distillation signal to the task and student capacity, and evaluating robustness and privacy implications.

papers_seen.author: Molina
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core of Model Compression — Powerful but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD delivers strong empirical gains in memory and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance, and it naturally extends beyond logits to include intermediate representations, attention maps, and synthesized inputs. However, KD is not a universal solution: optimization challenges, teacher–student capacity mismatch, limited or private data, and transfer of unwanted behaviors mean distillation must be treated as a design pattern within a broader compression pipeline. When combined with architecture-aware design, data strategies (including data-free synthesis), and complementary techniques such as pruning and quantization, KD reliably supports real-world deployment while demanding careful, task-aware choices to avoid failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Lyons
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and natural language processing. The family of KD methods spans soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate representation and attention imitation, multi-teacher and ensemble-derived strategies, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or co-distillation schemes. Successful application requires careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, whether original data are available (or must be synthesized), and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical practice shows KD frequently yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, but open problems remain around robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare or domain-specific behaviors, theoretical understanding of transfer dynamics, and scalable private or data-free distillation.

papers_seen.author: Espinoza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Outcomes, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal signals from teachers. Over the past decade KD has broadened from simple soft-label matching to a diverse set of techniques — intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, data- or generator-based synthesis, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirically, distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and training dynamics. Open problems remain in robustness to domain shift, preserving rare-token fidelity in sequence tasks, privacy- and data-constrained distillation, and principled selection of distilled signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Payne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller students that can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD variants transfer soft targets, intermediate representations, attention patterns, or synthetic data, and they are often combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. While KD routinely produces strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks, its effectiveness depends on careful choices about the distilled signals, teacher–student compatibility, data provenance (including data-free settings), and training regimes to preserve robustness and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Dominguez
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a System-Level, Context-Dependent Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its value arises from flexible choices about what and how to transfer (logits, features, relational signals), how to expose students to informative inputs (real, synthesized, or online signals), and how to combine distillation with architecture and numerical compression. However, distillation is not automatic: teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability or privacy constraints, and deployment targets (latency, memory, robustness, fairness) materially affect outcomes. Viewing distillation as a system-level primitive — one part of a broader compression and deployment pipeline — yields better, more reliable trade-offs between efficiency and retained capability.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Understanding and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. It encompasses soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and training-time adaptations that account for student capacity and deployment constraints. In practice KD is combined with complementary methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, and data-free synthesis) to meet latency, memory, or privacy requirements. KD is effective across vision, language, generative models, and view- or modality-specific tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student compatibility, available data, and careful choice of distillation objectives and schedules; open challenges remain in robustness, rare-token behavior, fairness, and theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, Practical Outcomes, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD encompasses matching softened output distributions, aligning intermediate representations and attention maps, ensembling or progressive teacher schedules, and operating under data constraints (including data-free or synthetic-data strategies). When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and student-aware design, KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing latency and memory. However, effectiveness depends on teacher–student alignment, data provenance and availability, and training protocols; KD can propagate teacher errors (particularly for rare tokens/classes), degrade under distribution shift, and incur extra training overhead unless efficiency techniques are applied. Best practice treats KD as a flexible pipeline: choose appropriate distillation targets, reconcile architectural mismatches, use data strategies that match deployment constraints, and combine KD with other compression and robustness-aware methods.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches and Insights in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer useful information from larger, more expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, deployable models. Research spans theoretical analyses of what is transferred, architectural and loss-design strategies to improve feature and output matching, specialized teacher–student training regimes (including multi-teacher and student-aware teacher training), online and federated distillation for large-scale or privacy-sensitive settings, and structural compression strategies that preserve accuracy while reducing memory and compute. Applications include image models, generative models, question-answering systems and multi-task natural language understanding, with methods tailored to domain constraints such as heterogeneous device capabilities and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from large teacher models or ensembles to smaller student models to reduce inference cost and memory while preserving task performance. The field encompasses soft-label (logit) supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, structural and architectural transformations, data-free and privacy-aware variants, multi-teacher and online distillation, and meta-learned teacher strategies. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often improves student generalization and enables deployment under resource constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on what signals are transferred, data availability and provenance, optimization dynamics, and teacher–student capacity gaps. Practical deployment requires choosing student architectures, distillation signals, and training regimes aligned to the target task and constraints; key open problems include robust data-free distillation, principled teacher design, and theoretical characterization of when different knowledge sources help.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transform large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster, and more deployable models while attempting to preserve accuracy and useful inductive biases. Approaches span classic teacher–student logit matching, representation and feature imitation, layer mapping strategies for large pretrained language models, data-free and zero-shot methods that avoid access to original training data, and privacy- or communication-aware frameworks for distributed settings. Empirical work demonstrates these methods can yield practical speedups, substantial parameter reductions, and competitive task performance across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks; theoretical and empirical studies also clarify when softened teacher targets or distilled datasets best help student capacity. Remaining challenges include balancing privacy and utility, reducing the cost of distillation when teachers are large, and extending guarantees and methods across modalities and domain shifts.

papers_seen.author: Orr
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The approach spans logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, self-distillation, multi-teacher and data-free variants, and combinations with structural compression such as pruning and quantization. KD is effective across modalities and tasks but its empirical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and training dynamics; open challenges remain in preserving rare-token behavior, robustness, privacy, and heterogeneous architecture transfer.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller ones by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from a teacher to a student. Over the past decade KD methods have diversified beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher pipelines, data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical work across NLP, speech, vision-language, and other domains shows KD can preserve most of a teacher's performance while drastically reducing model size and latency. Theoretical and empirical analyses have clarified why KD works in many settings (regularization via soft targets, ensemble-induced dark knowledge, and representation enrichment), but open problems remain in data privacy, distribution shift, automated student design, and guarantees for out-of-distribution robustness.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of teacher performance. Research across vision, speech, translation, and NLP tasks has developed multiple KD objectives (soft logits, intermediate-feature matching, attention or projector-based alignment), training regimes (offline teacher–student, self-distillation, multi-teacher, adversarial transfer), and data strategies (data-free, distilled datasets, and hybrid authentic/synthetic training). Empirical and theoretical work explains why KD often improves student generalization (dark-knowledge regularization, transferred inductive biases) while also documenting limitations (capacity mismatch, teacher error propagation, distributional/low-frequency failures) and practical remedies. Best practice is to treat KD as a flexible toolkit and combine it with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A diverse set of KD mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature alignment, attention- and relation-based signals, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data synthesis—has been developed and combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many vision and language tasks, while remaining sensitive to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, domain shift, and robustness concerns. Practical pipelines therefore co-design student architectures, distillation targets, and data handling strategies to achieve the best trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers information beyond hard labels—soft logits, intermediate representations, attention patterns, and relational signals—to enable substantial reductions in size and latency while preserving much teacher performance. Its success in practice depends on careful choice of distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data strategies (including synthetic or data-free approaches), and complementary compression methods. KD is powerful but not universal: optimization mismatch, domain shift, and limited data can undermine transfer, so robust pipelines co-design student architectures, distillation signals, and training/data workflows to realize production gains.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce inference cost while retaining performance. A broad family of approaches—from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher ensembles, data-free synthesis, and federated or privacy-aware protocols—enables deployment across vision, speech, and language tasks. Practical success depends on matching the distillation signal to student capacity, combining KD with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, pretraining), and addressing data, optimization, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques that transfer information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD methods differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational structure) and how training proceeds (offline teacher supervision, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, or data-free synthesis). Practical deployments combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and require attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability, and task-specific choices. Empirical evidence shows KD reliably yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks, but success depends on optimization dynamics, the choice of distilled signals, and constraints such as access to original training data or deployment hardware.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Travis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical First-Line Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. By transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone (softened logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, ensemble consensus), and by combining distillation with data strategies and complementary compression techniques, KD routinely produces compact models that meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: careful selection of distillation signals, teacher–student alignment, data augmentation or synthesis, and evaluation under realistic distribution shifts are necessary to avoid failure modes. Treated as a system-level pipeline rather than a single loss, KD is the recommended first-line strategy for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Targeted Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable strategy for producing compact, deployable models by transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller students. The field has evolved beyond matching softened output logits to include representation-level guidance, attention and relational targets, data-augmentation and synthesis strategies, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision and language shows that appropriately designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance while reducing compute, memory, and latency; however, success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and provenance, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as one component of a compression toolkit, integrating architecture choices, precision reductions, and data strategies to meet production constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically effective approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster students for deployment. When combined with complementary compression techniques and task-aware choices about what and how to transfer, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. At the same time, careful attention to data availability, teacher–student mismatch, and domain shift is required to preserve robustness and rare or domain-specific behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for converting large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, and multimodal settings KD has been shown to recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost and memory footprint. The technique comprises multiple transfer targets (soft outputs/logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure) and schedules (offline teacher supervision, online co-training, multi-teacher ensembles). Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design, and must attend to data availability, teacher-student capacity alignment, and distributional robustness. Open challenges include data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, reliable transfer under domain shift, preserving rare-token or fine-grained behaviors in NLP, and mitigating transfer of biases or teacher errors.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a set of techniques for transferring behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller student models so the students can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target (logit) matching to a broad family of objectives that include intermediate representation matching, attention- and relational-level transfer, ensemble-to-single distillation, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants. In practice KD is most effective when its signals are chosen to match student capacity and the deployment setting, and when it is combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and appropriate data strategies. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or fine-grained behavior (especially in NLP), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and preserving robustness and fairness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Multi‑Strategy Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach to compressing large models into smaller, efficient students. When treated as a toolbox of complementary methods—logit-level supervision, representation matching, layer alignment, multi-teacher schedules, data synthesis, and privacy-aware mechanisms—KD enables compact models to approach the performance of larger teachers while meeting real-world constraints on latency, memory, and data access. At the same time, distillation outcomes depend on teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices; addressing these limits requires careful method selection and integration with complementary compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of methods for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD encompasses logit-level soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational or ensemble signals, and many practical variants (online, self-distillation, data-free). When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student co-design, KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for classification, sequence tasks, retrieval, and generative systems. However, KD is not universally effective: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and distributional match, and the choice of distillation signals; open problems include reliable distillation without original data, preserving low-frequency or rare behaviors in NLP, and avoiding transfer of undesirable properties such as biases or fragility.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, broadly applicable family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their predictive power. KD enables large gains in inference speed, reduced memory footprint, and practical deployment under latency, compute, and privacy constraints. However, straightforward distillation can transfer undesirable properties and can underperform when data is limited or teacher–student mismatches are large. To realize KD's full potential practitioners should combine soft-target transfer with representation matching, targeted data augmentation or data-free synthesis, careful teacher design (including ensembles or student-aware teachers), and explicit robustness or privacy-aware objectives. These combined practices produce compact models that are accurate, efficient, and more robust for real-world NLP and deep-learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Castaneda
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Patterns, and Practical Caveats
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile toolkit that transfers richer supervision from larger or heterogeneous teacher models into smaller students to reduce inference cost while retaining task performance. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals), composes with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design), and can be adapted to domain-specific settings (generative models, recommenders, distributed training). Its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data alignment, choice of signals to transfer, and mitigation strategies for robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy. When applied with principled design—matching distilled signals to student capacity, using teacher-aware curricula, and combining with other compression tools—KD frequently yields production-ready efficiency gains, but it is not a universal remedy and requires careful engineering to avoid failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Empirical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Approaches extend beyond matching soft logits to include intermediate-feature mimicry, attention-driven layer alignment, many-to-many layer mapping, contrastive representation alignment, and task- or domain-aware search and adaptation. Empirical work shows KD is effective across modalities and tasks — from pre-trained language models and visual-linguistic systems to object detectors, recommender rankers, graph networks, and continual learning settings — but practical deployment requires addressing representation misalignment, task specificity, and catastrophic forgetting. This review synthesizes core strategies and key empirical findings to guide application and future research.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Context‑Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical route to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD is both a compression mechanism and a training-time regularizer: when carefully designed it preserves much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost. However, KD’s success depends on choices about what to transfer (outputs, intermediate features, or both), how to align teacher and student architectures, what data are used (real, augmented, or synthetic), and whether deployment constraints (privacy, heterogeneity, federated settings) limit access to teacher data or models. A principled KD practice adapts targets, aligns representations where useful, addresses teacher–student mismatches, and recognizes scenarios where KD alone is insufficient.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD methods differ in what is transferred (softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals) and in training protocols (offline teacher supervision, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants). In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and when practitioner choices account for teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and target-task constraints. While KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision and language tasks, its limitations include sensitivity to optimization dynamics, degradation on rare or safety-critical behaviors, and challenges in data-free or privacy-constrained settings. The field offers pragmatic recipes—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning representations, and using data or synthetic surrogates—that produce deployable compact models, but outstanding research questions remain about principled teacher design, robustness under distribution shift, and data-free distillation quality.

papers_seen.author: Dean
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels. Over the past decade KD has evolved from soft-label matching to a family of methods that include feature- and attention-level imitation, layer mapping and projection, multi-teacher and online schedules, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, and combinations with structural compression such as pruning and quantization. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers much of a teacher’s performance while reducing inference cost, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and provenance, and careful design choices about which signals to transfer. Open challenges include handling distribution shift, preserving rare-class or rare-token behavior, and avoiding propagation of teacher errors or undesirable behaviors. This synthesis summarizes common methods, mechanisms, practical patterns, and outstanding limitations to guide researchers and practitioners applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a General-Purpose Compression Strategy for Deep Models: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a specialized technique for transferring softened output distributions into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing and adapting deep models across domains (vision, language, multimodal, and generative models). Empirical results across tasks show that KD can preserve or even improve accuracy while substantially reducing model size and latency, and it can be combined with complementary strategies (pre-training, low-precision arithmetic, data synthesis, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints and privacy requirements. However, effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, attention maps), how teachers and students are aligned (layer mapping, input alignment), and whether real data are available (data-free or adversarially guided generation). This paper synthesizes evidence from recent work to argue that KD, when applied with these considerations, is a reliable foundation for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile approach that compresses large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble consensus. KD enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance across modalities (NLP, speech, vision) and tasks. Its practical success depends on the choice of distilled signals, data strategies, and teacher-student design; when combined with augmentation, ensemble guidance, or privacy-aware mechanisms, KD supports real-world deployment while requiring safeguards against bias, privacy leakage, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated pathway to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. KD encompasses multiple forms of transferred knowledge (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and operates across modes (offline, online, ensemble, data-free). When co‑designed with student architectures and combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs for vision and language models. However, practical success requires attention to teacher–student compatibility, data availability and provenance, and robustness to domain shift and rare behaviors. The method is best treated as a default, context‑aware tool that should be adapted—rather than assumed universal—for each deployment setting.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students for deployment in constrained environments. KD can transfer predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and structural inductive biases; it supports multi-teacher, progressive, adversarial, and data-constrained variants; and it can be combined with architecture-aware design and data strategies to improve efficiency, robustness, and domain adaptability. While highly effective in practice, KD's success depends on choices about what to transfer, how teachers and students are aligned, and the availability and suitability of data, so it should be treated as a flexible toolkit rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. The literature frames KD as a multifaceted toolkit—ranging from logit-level soft-target matching to representation- and attention-level alignment, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware procedures, and compositions with structural compression such as pruning and quantization. Empirical work shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in memory and latency, but success depends on teacher–student compatibility, availability and quality of data, and careful selection of distillation signals and optimization protocols. Practical pipelines therefore combine multiple KD strategies with complementary compression techniques and task-aware adaptations to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces the cost of deploying large deep models by transferring information from high-capacity teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of KD variants—soft-target matching, internal-feature and attention matching, multi-teacher or ensemble guidance, online and meta-learned teaching, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches—enable tradeoffs among size, latency, and retained performance. Practical deployments commonly combine KD with architecture-aware transformations (pruning, quantization, architecture redesign), data-management strategies, and training schedules to address constraints such as limited data, device heterogeneity, privacy, and fairness. While KD often produces strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices about what and how to transfer, student capacity and architecture, and the provenance of training data; persistent challenges include domain shift, teacher errors, preserving rare behaviors, and avoiding unintentional transfer of bias.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), how teachers and students are aligned, and how data (real, synthetic, or absent) are handled, KD routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when practitioners explicitly address robustness, fairness, and distributional mismatch. However, KD is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the choice of distillation signal determine success, and careful objective design and evaluation are required to avoid propagating teacher errors or amplifying undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features/attention, relational or structural signals) and can be applied in offline, online, ensemble, or data-constrained settings. Empirical results across vision, speech, and language show that appropriately designed distillation pipelines can deliver large efficiency gains with modest loss (and sometimes gains) in accuracy, but success depends on choices about what is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical deployments typically combine KD with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and require design attention to robustness, domain shift, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the last decade KD has diversified from soft-target matching to include intermediate representation and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. Practical compression typically combines KD with architecture-aware transformations (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies; success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data provenance, and important open problems remain in robustness, fairness, and cross-domain generalization.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Powerful but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what teacher signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity and inputs, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods—KD routinely reduces model size and latency while preserving much task performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, optimization dynamics, and task-specific phenomena (e.g., rare-token behavior), so careful protocol design and evaluation under realistic constraints are essential.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expressive models to smaller, efficient models to enable practical deployment without excessive loss in performance. These methods include matching teacher soft outputs, feature-level alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and architecture-aware strategies for heterogeneous settings. Across domains—vision, speech, NLP, and recommender systems—distillation is used both to compress models for latency and memory constraints and to inject complementary knowledge (e.g., cross-task or cross-modal signals). Empirical work shows that careful design choices (e.g., mixing hard/soft targets, projector modules, or student-aware teacher training) and task-specific adaptations address common pitfalls such as information loss on rare tokens or domain shifts. Open directions include stronger theoretical understanding, robustness under imperfect teachers, and principled integration with quantization, federated settings, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mckee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and distributed settings KD often recovers much of a teacher's predictive performance while enabling faster inference, lower memory use, and deployment under resource or privacy constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: outcomes depend on what signals are transferred (logits, features, attention), teacher–student compatibility, availability and quality of data (including data-free or federated setups), and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Best practice treats distillation as one element of a compression pipeline that combines representation matching, architecture-aware student design, data strategies, and risk-aware training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large deep models into compact ones that are suitable for deployment. Across NLP, speech, vision-language, and specialized tasks such as machine reading comprehension, KD enables students to inherit performance-critical behaviors from larger teachers while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in model size and compute. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., architecture search or structured pruning) and when tailored to task or domain specifics, distillation yields compressed models that approach teacher performance while meeting resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.
