papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Multifaceted, and Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their predictive power. When combined with complementary strategies—task-aware objectives, intermediate representation matching, online or distributed schemes, and teacher-student co-design—KD supports deployment on resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive environments. Nonetheless, its effectiveness depends strongly on teacher-student capacity alignment, data availability (including few-shot or data-free regimes), and the choice of distilled signals; recognizing these dependencies leads to principled best practices that balance fidelity, robustness, and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target (logit) transfer into a broad toolkit that also includes intermediate representation matching, attention- and layer-aware objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with structural compression. Practical deployments of KD require careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited or no access to original training data. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss in many settings, open problems remain in robustness under distribution shift, privacy- and data-constrained regimes, and principled selection of distilled signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. When KD is treated as a context-aware toolkit—selecting what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques—it enables substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. However, success requires careful attention to architecture heterogeneity, data availability, domain specifics, and evaluation of robustness and rare-class behavior.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated pathway to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. KD encompasses multiple forms of transferred knowledge (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and operates across modes (offline, online, ensemble, data-free). When co‑designed with student architectures and combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs for vision and language models. However, practical success requires attention to teacher–student compatibility, data availability and provenance, and robustness to domain shift and rare behaviors. The method is best treated as a default, context‑aware tool that should be adapted—rather than assumed universal—for each deployment setting.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large neural networks for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Beyond simple model-size reduction, KD enables transfer of inductive biases, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving distributed training, data-free and zero-shot compression, and the transfer of adversarial robustness. Combining logit-based distillation with feature-level mimicking and carefully chosen regularization yields high-quality small models that remain competitive on downstream tasks in NLP and broader deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically effective approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster students for deployment. When combined with complementary compression techniques and task-aware choices about what and how to transfer, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. At the same time, careful attention to data availability, teacher–student mismatch, and domain shift is required to preserve robustness and rare or domain-specific behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Mckee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and distributed settings KD often recovers much of a teacher's predictive performance while enabling faster inference, lower memory use, and deployment under resource or privacy constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: outcomes depend on what signals are transferred (logits, features, attention), teacher–student compatibility, availability and quality of data (including data-free or federated setups), and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Best practice treats distillation as one element of a compression pipeline that combines representation matching, architecture-aware student design, data strategies, and risk-aware training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Trade-offs, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- or resource-constrained settings. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, researchers have developed logit-based distillation, feature- and attention-level mimicking, ensemble- and multi-teacher schemes, task-adaptive compression, and data- or teacher-free variants. These methods trade off compute, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness, and are often complementary to pruning and architecture search. Practical adoption favors combinations of pretraining, targeted distillation objectives, and adaptations to mismatches between teacher and student (e.g., inputs or architecture).

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones that are deployable in resource-constrained settings. A rich set of distillation strategies has been developed: matching teacher output distributions, transferring intermediate representations, adversarial or data-free synthesis of training examples, multi-teacher aggregation, and contrastive or projector-based representation alignment. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many tasks (including NLP and graph learning), but practical success depends strongly on optimization details, the availability and alignment of data, and careful design of the distillation objective. Privacy-preserving variants and methods tailored to domain-specific architectures (e.g., GNNs, transformers) extend KD’s applicability, while also introducing trade-offs between utility, robustness, and guarantees. This synthesis summarizes key methods, empirical findings, and known limitations to guide research and practice in KD for deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, privacy, or device constraints. KD methods operate across multiple knowledge channels (soft logits, internal features, attention/relations, layer mappings), and they are often combined with complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or data synthesis). Empirical work shows distilled students can often recover the bulk of teacher performance while reducing compute and memory substantially, but effectiveness depends on task, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and distributional shifts. Important open problems remain in data-free distillation, few-shot compression, preserving rare-token behaviors and robustness, and designing distillation as a system-level primitive matched to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Lyons
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and natural language processing. The family of KD methods spans soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate representation and attention imitation, multi-teacher and ensemble-derived strategies, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or co-distillation schemes. Successful application requires careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, whether original data are available (or must be synthesized), and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical practice shows KD frequently yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, but open problems remain around robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare or domain-specific behaviors, theoretical understanding of transfer dynamics, and scalable private or data-free distillation.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other forms of teacher knowledge. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled practical reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on what form of knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student representations are aligned, the availability and selection of data for distillation, and complementary compression techniques such as low-precision numerics, pruning, or architecture adaptation. Remaining challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, reliable distillation without original data, robustness and fairness under compression, and principled methods for matching heterogeneous teacher–student pairs.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and language. A diverse set of distillation recipes—soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, self- and online-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and data-free synthesis—enables trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy. Success depends on co-designing teacher and student architectures, selecting appropriate transfer signals, handling data availability or privacy constraints, and integrating complementary compression methods. Remaining gaps include robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or safety-critical behaviors, and principled theory to predict when particular distillation strategies will succeed in production.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Current Understandings of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used model compression paradigm in which a smaller student model is trained to capture the behavior of a larger teacher model. It has been applied across domains (vision, NLP, recommender systems, medical imaging) to reduce model size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Work in the field explores what is transferred (soft outputs, internal representations, feature relations), how to improve transfer (adversarial samples, contrastive objectives, structural transformations), and how to address practical constraints (absence of original data, domain shift, privacy, fairness and robustness). Empirical results show KD often yields substantial memory and runtime benefits with modest accuracy loss and can be combined with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Yet KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, imperfect teacher signals, and mismatches between teacher and student capacity can limit how closely a student matches a teacher; research continues into theoretical explanations and robust, data-efficient methods.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile technique for shrinking large neural models while preserving much of their predictive power. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and easier deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings. When combined with teacher ensembles, online or self-distillation, task-adaptive search, and careful handling of soft labels and data augmentation, distillation can deliver near-teacher accuracy while addressing scalability, robustness, and domain transfer concerns. I argue that knowledge distillation should be a first-line approach for model compression in modern NLP pipelines, supplemented by principled choices about teachers, data, and optimization to realize its full benefits.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Wang
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Practice, Mechanisms, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, practical toolkit for producing compact, faster models from large neural teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD methods extend beyond soft-target matching to include intermediate-feature and attention alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware or data-free strategies. In practice, distillation is most effective when combined with architecture-aware design and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization); careful choice of what to transfer, how to align layers, and what data to use is critical. Remaining challenges include reliably preserving rare-token behavior, robustness and fairness under compression, data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, and principled co-design of teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Day
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible, empirically supported path to compress large models into compact, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. When treated as a central design pattern rather than a single loss term, KD enables multiple transfer targets (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention, relational signals), multi-teacher and online schedules, and integration with architecture-aware design and other compression methods. Practical success requires explicit attention to teacher–student alignment, data strategies (including pre-training of compact architectures and data augmentation or synthesis), and theoretical understanding of when soft versus hard supervision helps. Framed this way, KD is the most practical, multi-strategy mechanism for real-world compression, provided practitioners pair it with complementary techniques and careful evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a flexible, practical toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and language tasks, KD transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from teachers to students using a variety of signals and training regimes. In practice KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), appropriate data strategies (pretraining, data synthesis, or online sharing), and careful teacher–student design. The technique yields strong efficiency gains but requires attention to capacity mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from large teacher models or ensembles to smaller student models to reduce inference cost and memory while preserving task performance. The field encompasses soft-label (logit) supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, structural and architectural transformations, data-free and privacy-aware variants, multi-teacher and online distillation, and meta-learned teacher strategies. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often improves student generalization and enables deployment under resource constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on what signals are transferred, data availability and provenance, optimization dynamics, and teacher–student capacity gaps. Practical deployment requires choosing student architectures, distillation signals, and training regimes aligned to the target task and constraints; key open problems include robust data-free distillation, principled teacher design, and theoretical characterization of when different knowledge sources help.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other forms of teacher knowledge. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled practical reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on what form of knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student representations are aligned, the availability and selection of data for distillation, and complementary compression techniques such as low-precision numerics, pruning, or architecture adaptation. Remaining challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, reliable distillation without original data, robustness and fairness under compression, and principled methods for matching heterogeneous teacher–student pairs.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When combined with complementary practices—such as pretraining compact students, representation-level matching, curriculum scheduling, teacher ensembles, and data augmentation—KD yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and performance across modalities and tasks. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data or domain mismatch; KD therefore functions best as a central, flexible component within a broader compression pipeline rather than as a one-size-fits-all cure.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models so that students retain much of the teachers' task performance while reducing inference cost and resource consumption. The practice extends beyond matching final logits to include feature- and layer-level supervision, attention- or projector-based alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware strategies (including data-free or synthetic-data approaches). KD has been applied across modalities and deployment regimes (on-device, privacy-aware, and distributed/federated settings), and empirical work highlights both practical successes and recurring failure modes such as sensitivity to teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, and preservation of rare or low-frequency signals. Current best practices emphasize combining representation-level objectives, careful input/data handling, and co-design of teacher and student; open problems remain around robustness, heterogeneity, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Travis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical First-Line Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. By transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone (softened logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, ensemble consensus), and by combining distillation with data strategies and complementary compression techniques, KD routinely produces compact models that meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: careful selection of distillation signals, teacher–student alignment, data augmentation or synthesis, and evaluation under realistic distribution shifts are necessary to avoid failure modes. Treated as a system-level pipeline rather than a single loss, KD is the recommended first-line strategy for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, high-impact approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. KD succeeds because it can transfer diverse forms of information—soft outputs, internal representations, relational structure—and because it composes naturally with complementary techniques (pretraining, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, and multi-teacher ensembles). When applied with attention to teacher quality, data alignment, and student pretraining, KD enables practical, resource-aware deployments across vision, speech, and language tasks. This paper argues KD should often be the first method considered for compression, and outlines core mechanisms, practical recipes, and remaining challenges for robust application in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. A broad family of KD methods transfers teacher behavior through soft-label matching, intermediate representation alignment, attention- or task-aware layer projection, ensemble/online schemes, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols. When combined with architecture search, progressive module replacement, or data synthesis, KD enables strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs that make large pretrained models practical for edge, federated, and privacy-sensitive deployments. Key practical decisions include what form of knowledge to transfer, how to align mismatched teacher and student representations, and how to handle limited or no access to original training data. Remaining challenges center on teacher–student compatibility, data heterogeneity, robustness under compression, and principled selection of distilled signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Carpenter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone of Model Compression: Capabilities, Variants, and Contextual Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD supports a broad set of objectives—matching logits, aligning internal representations, using online or multi-teacher schemes, and operating with or without original training data—so it serves as the backbone of many modern compression pipelines. However, its success is context-dependent: choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability, and deployment constraints determine outcomes, and KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques and principled training workflows.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for converting large neural teachers into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when applied thoughtfully, but it is not a standalone solution: real-world compression requires attention to what is transferred, teacher–student capacity alignment, data provenance and availability, robustness and safety concerns, and the coordinated use of complementary compression methods such as architecture search, pruning, and curriculum or data strategies. Treating KD as a system-level primitive and combining it with targeted interventions produces the most reliable, efficient, and robust compressed models for production NLP and deep learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or complex models into smaller, faster, or more constrained students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from a teacher. Over the past decade this has produced a diverse set of recipes — from logits/soft-label supervision to feature and layer-wise matching, progressive module replacement, data-free or privacy-aware distillation, and distributed/online variants — that together address deployment, privacy, robustness, and resource heterogeneity. Empirical work demonstrates that distilled students can approach teacher performance in NLP and vision tasks while enabling faster inference, lower memory use, or operation on weak devices; theoretical and empirical analyses illuminate when soft labels help, when hard labels or sample selection are needed, and how augmentation or task-aware selection of teacher knowledge improves transfer. Remaining challenges include principled understanding of which teacher signals are most useful for a given target task and resource constraint, robust and private distillation without original data, and scalable distillation in large distributed training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring supervisory signals richer than hard labels. Across vision, language, graph, and generative modeling, KD has matured into a flexible toolkit that includes logit-level supervision, intermediate-feature matching, relational or attention alignment, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware variants. In practice KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and when the distillation protocol is chosen to match student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints. Open challenges remain in data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, preserving rare-token and long-tail behaviors, avoiding propagation of undesirable teacher behaviors (biases or brittleness), and guaranteeing robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Mathis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks. The literature frames KD as a family of techniques—soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and task-aware losses—combined with varied training regimes (offline, online, self-distillation, multi-teacher) and deployment-aware integrations (pretraining, architecture-aware adapters, pruning, quantization, and data augmentation). Empirical and theoretical studies show KD often preserves much of a teacher’s performance while reducing parameter count and latency, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the choice of what and how to transfer. Ongoing challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, handling heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or domain-specific signals, and reducing the computational cost of distillation itself.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile technique for shrinking large neural models while preserving much of their predictive power. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and easier deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings. When combined with teacher ensembles, online or self-distillation, task-adaptive search, and careful handling of soft labels and data augmentation, distillation can deliver near-teacher accuracy while addressing scalability, robustness, and domain transfer concerns. I argue that knowledge distillation should be a first-line approach for model compression in modern NLP pipelines, supplemented by principled choices about teachers, data, and optimization to realize its full benefits.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic training trick into a unifying framework for producing compact, efficient models across vision, speech, and language tasks. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble consensus from larger teachers to smaller students, KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while largely preserving accuracy. Beyond plain size reduction, KD adapts to constraints that arise in real deployments — limited data or privacy-sensitive settings, heterogeneous architectures, and modality gaps — through techniques such as feature-level alignment, selective sampling, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and data-free synthesis. As a practical bridge between research-scale architectures and deployable systems, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and serves both as an efficiency accelerator and as a lever for robustness and domain generalization.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single teacher→student soft-label transfer into a broad toolkit for compressing and adapting deep models across vision, language, and multimodal domains. Contemporary approaches extend logits matching to representation- and structure-aware objectives, multi- and continual-teaching schemes, task-aware layer selection, and combinations with pruning or architecture-level compression. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints but its success depends on design choices about what is transferred, how the student is supervised, data availability, and student capacity. Practical progress emphasizes representation matching beyond logits, careful layer- and channel-level alignment, and composing KD with other compression techniques; remaining challenges include robustness under distribution shift, data-free scenarios, and preserving fine-grained or safety-critical behavior.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. KD has been applied successfully to compress large language models, vision transformers, and task-specific architectures, and adapted to settings including self-supervision, multi-task learning, and privacy-sensitive or data-limited regimes. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on the alignment between teacher and student architectures, the availability and quality of data (or of synthetic surrogates), the selection of what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention, relational signals), and task-specific choices such as layer-wise matching and curriculum. Recognizing both the demonstrated strengths and the practical failure modes of KD leads to targeted best practices: choose distillation targets that match the student capacity and task, use task-aware or feature-focused objectives for intermediate representations, apply adversarial or synthetic data approaches when original data are unavailable, and explicitly evaluate KD under realistic heterogeneity (e.g., federated or multi-task) to avoid hidden degradations.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, or privacy constraints. The literature has converged on a set of recurring methods (soft-target/logit supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware protocols) and deployment practices (combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search). Empirical evidence demonstrates that appropriately designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional alignment. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors (especially in NLP), and principled teacher–student co-design and curricula for difficult tasks.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and versatile approach for shrinking high-capacity models into smaller, deployable models while retaining much of their performance. When applied thoughtfully — with attention to what to transfer (logits, features, intermediate representations), how to align teachers and students (layer mapping, task-aware filters), and how to handle data constraints (data-free synthesis, federated heterogeneity, privacy) — KD enables latency- and memory-efficient deployment across vision, language, multimodal, and generative settings. However, KD is not automatic: its success depends on teacher–student capacity matching, the choice of distilled signals, and addressing data heterogeneity or absence. The evidence suggests KD should be treated as a flexible toolkit combined with complementary strategies (architecture search, quantization, data augmentation) to meet real deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation in Modern Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a foundational technique for compressing large neural models while retaining much of their performance. Across vision and language tasks, distillation can act both as a compression mechanism and as a regularizer, and it integrates naturally with complementary strategies such as architecture search, layer-wise alignment, representation matching, data augmentation, pruning, and deployment-aware methods. When applied thoughtfully—matching teacher and student representations, tuning the signal provided by soft labels, and adapting to task or device constraints—distillation enables practical, high-performing compressed models suitable for production and edge settings.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels — output logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure — and are commonly combined with architecture-level compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and training strategies (online co-training, curriculum schedules, synthetic-data protocols). Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while improving latency and memory usage, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and appropriate choice of transfer signal. Ongoing challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, and operating in data-limited or privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural teachers into smaller student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, KD techniques include soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention- or relation-based alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher fusion, and data- or domain-aware variations. Empirical work shows that distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet deployment constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and training objectives. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, transferring robustness and inductive biases, and handling heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive environments.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models so that the students retain much of the teachers' performance while meeting resource, latency, or privacy constraints. KD methods include matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations or attention, synthesizing surrogate training data when original data are unavailable, and deploying progressive or ensemble-based strategies. Practical pipelines commonly combine KD with architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or search) and training-time strategies (curricula, online distillation, or federated protocols) to balance efficiency and accuracy. Despite strong empirical success across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in aligning heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, operating under limited or private data, and designing principled objectives and curricula that preserve robustness and task-specific inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Santana
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD encompasses multiple transfer mechanisms (soft-targets, intermediate representation matching, relational and attention-based transfers, and data-side interventions) and is most effective when treated as a toolkit combined with complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on teacher quality, data availability (including data-free or synthetic strategies), teacher–student capacity alignment, and robustness considerations. A principled KD practice adapts the transfer signals to task and data regimes, uses multi-teacher or data-synthesis techniques when needed, and explicitly pairs distillation with deployment-aware compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their predictive power. Across vision, language, and generative settings, KD extends from simple softened-logit matching to richer objectives that mimic intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure; it also supports varied training regimes including offline teacher–student, online co-training, multi-teacher curricula, and data-free synthesis. When combined with complementary methods (pretraining, architecture search, pruning, quantization, and federated procedures), KD helps meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints in real deployments. However, success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align architectures, how to handle limited or absent data, and how to avoid transferring undesirable teacher behaviors—issues that remain active research directions.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is the most practical, flexible, and widely applied approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and language tasks. KD brings together soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware strategies into a single, adaptable pipeline that can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet real-world deployment constraints. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, its reliability depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these concerns makes KD a central component of robust, system-level compression workflows rather than a one-shot recipe.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a simple teacher-student training recipe into a multifaceted toolkit that enables efficient, robust, and privacy-aware deployment of deep models. KD not only compresses large models into faster, smaller students suitable for edge and production, but also enables task-adaptive compression, data-limited or data-free scenarios, privacy-preserving federated setups, and transfers of inductive biases across architectures. When combined with complementary techniques such as architecture search, specialized feature-matching losses, and careful input-side interventions, KD yields practical compressed models without prohibitive losses in accuracy and can improve generalization in out-of-distribution settings.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit—logit-level supervision, intermediate-feature matching, layer-mapping, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware or data-free variants—has been developed to meet deployment constraints in vision and natural language tasks. Empirical work shows that, when combined with architecture-aware choices and complementary compression techniques, KD frequently yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance, though careful method selection is required to mitigate mismatches, data limitations, and task-specific failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or multi-modal models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural insights. Research has developed diverse KD variants—soft-label distillation, internal and layer-wise imitation, task-aware filtering, data-free distillation, and architecture-search guided compression—each addressing optimization, data availability, or deployment constraints. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs between matching teacher outputs and student generalization, the value of pre-training compact models, and the importance of choosing what and how knowledge is transferred to maximize downstream task performance while meeting resource limits.
